metaDescription: Four Ooni pizza ovens compared: Koda 2, Koda 2 Pro, Karu 12 and Volt 2, with honest notes on fuel, size, stone design and who each model suits.
expertTake: The Ooni Koda 2 is the pick for most buyers because its thicker stone and propane burner make back-to-back pies easy without any fire skills. The Karu 12 is the pick for people who want real wood or charcoal and may add gas later. Anyone who needs an indoor oven should buy the Volt 2 and skip the three outdoor models, which must never run inside.
introParagraphs: A single brand can sell very different machines under one name, and this brand is a clear case. The lineup spans gas, wood, multi-fuel and electric ovens, and the right choice depends on where you cook and how much attention you are willing to give a flame.

This guide compares four current models so you can match the fuel, size and setting to your space. It explains how each design heats the stone, what that means for the second and third pie, and which owners will be happiest after a year of use.

products.name: Ooni Koda 2 Propane Gas Pizza Oven, 14 Inch
products.description:
The Koda 2 is a propane-only oven that connects to a gas bottle through a 28 mBar regulator and hose. Its stone is described as 50 percent thicker than the previous generation, which stores more heat and shortens the wait between pies. That is the right engineering priority, because recovery between bakes decides how many pizzas a host can serve.

The tradeoff is fuel flexibility. Propane only means no wood option, so someone who wants a live fire should look at the Karu 12. The listing also stresses the 28 mBar regulator, so confirm that the regulator and hose match your tank connection before you order. Compared with the Koda 2 Pro, it is smaller and lighter, and it costs less.

Cover the oven when not in use, brush the stone after cooling and inspect the hose each season. The five year voluntary warranty is a reasonable sign of confidence. It suits buyers who want fast, repeatable pizza nights. Mount it on a flat, heat-rated table at a comfortable working height, and keep a long turning peel within reach, because a 14 inch pie leaves less room to maneuver than the specs suggest, and a bumpy surface will rock the stone.
products.bestFor: Hosts who want repeatable gas pizza with fast recovery between pies.
pros: Stone is fifty percent thicker for better recovery
Simple propane operation with regulator included
Fourteen inch chamber handles larger pies
Five year voluntary warranty from the maker
cons: Propane only, with no wood option
Regulator spec needs checking against your tank

products.name: Ooni Koda 2 Pro Propane Gas Pizza Oven, 18 Inch
products.description:
The Pro stretches the Koda 2 design to an 18 inch chamber and adds an expanded temperature range from 320F to 950F, which opens the oven to roasting and slow bakes. The Ooni Connect Digital Temperature Hub gives real-time ambient temperature and food probe readings. Those features turn it from a pizza oven into a broader outdoor cooker.

The tradeoff is size and cost. An 18 inch chamber needs a sturdy table, and it is the heaviest and most expensive Ooni oven in this guide. It also stays propane only, so wood fans should look at the Karu 12. For a household that rarely bakes above 14 inches, the standard Koda 2 is the better value.

Keep the probe and hub dry, check the hose each season and brush the stone after every cooldown. It suits a host who wants room for large pies and the ability to roast meat. Because the Pro is so large, measure the table and the path to the patio before ordering, and plan a cover sized for its body, since a generic cover will not close properly around the hub and the wide shell.
products.bestFor: Hosts who want an 18 inch chamber and probe-assisted roasting.
pros: Eighteen inch chamber for large pies and roasts
Connect hub reads oven and food probe temperature
Same propane operation as the smaller Koda
cons: Propane only, with no wood option
Needs a sturdy table and permanent space

products.name: Ooni Karu 12 Multi-Fuel Pizza Oven, 12 Inch

specList.label: Fuel
specList.value: Wood or charcoal, gas with burner

products.description:
The Karu 12 burns wood or charcoal straight from the box, and it can be paired with an Ooni gas burner that is sold separately. A custom fuel tray maximizes airflow and delivers a blast of flame, and the oven claims a 60 second bake. That makes it the most flexible Ooni for someone who values a live fire.

The tradeoff is attention and ash. Wood requires feeding the fire, and a small firebox burns quickly. Against the Koda 2, it needs more skill but offers smoke flavor that propane cannot. It also lacks the thicker stone of the newer Koda, so recovery between pies takes longer.

Clear ash after every session and store dry fuel. Wear gloves when feeding the box. It is the right choice for a hobbyist who enjoys the ritual of lighting a fire. Store charcoal or wood in a dry bin and keep a small bucket for ash beside the oven, since the compact firebox fills quickly during a long evening and ash blocks the airflow that the custom tray depends on.
products.bestFor: Fire lovers who want wood or charcoal now and gas as an upgrade.
pros: Burns wood or charcoal straight from the box
Gas option is available with a separate burner
Custom fuel tray increases airflow and flame
Rated for a roughly sixty second bake
cons: Gas burner is a separate purchase
Needs ongoing fire feeding and ash cleanup
Stone is less heat-retentive than the newer Koda

products.name: Ooni Volt 2 Electric Indoor Pizza Oven
products.description:
The Volt 2 is the only Ooni here that belongs inside a kitchen. It plugs in, covers a wide range from 70F to 850F and uses a patent-pending adaptive Pizza Intelligence system to adjust temperature. That range lets it work as a countertop oven beyond pizza.

The tradeoff is that an electric oven cannot match the flame feel of its outdoor siblings, and its 850F ceiling is below the 950F of the Koda ovens. It also demands a dedicated outlet and counter space. For an apartment dweller, those limits are acceptable because it is the only Ooni that can legally and safely run indoors.

Wipe the chamber after each use, brush the stone after cooling and keep the cord clear of the hot shell. It suits a household with no outdoor space. Check the manual for clearance rules around the vents, and place it on a heat-safe board with space behind it, since the electronics sit near the elements and a crowded shelf will trap heat.
products.bestFor: Apartment kitchens that want the Ooni name without an open flame.
pros: Runs indoors on a standard outlet
Works as a countertop oven beyond pizza
cons: Peak of 850F trails the Koda ovens at 950F
Needs counter space and a good outlet
No live flame or smoke flavor

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Koda 2 and Koda 2 Pro run on propane only, the Karu 12 burns wood or charcoal with an optional gas burner, and the Volt 2 is electric. Only the Volt 2 is made for indoor use. Gas and wood ovens need open air and must never run in a garage or a covered porch. Pick the fuel after you pick the place.  Ask whether you really bake above 14 inches before paying for the bigger chamber, since most family pizzas fit in the smaller oven.  Remember that propane tank size also matters, since a small tank can run out mid-party and a spare is cheap insurance.

The Koda 2 lists a stone that is 50 percent thicker than before, which reduces the wait between pies. A thin stone cools fast under cold dough. The Karu 12 does not list this upgrade. Recovery matters most when you serve several pies in a row.  If you often host back-to-back, favor the thicker stone, because waiting four minutes between pies is the most common complaint among guests.  Both fuels reward good preparation, so keep tools and dough ready before the oven reaches temperature.

The Karu 12 takes 12 inches, the Koda 2 takes 14 inches and the Koda 2 Pro takes 18 inches. A larger chamber needs more space and a stronger burner. The mistake is paying for 18 inches when you bake for two.  A pie that is too big for the chamber leaves little room for the peel, so size the dough to the oven, not the other way around.  Remember that a larger oven also takes longer to heat from cold, so allow extra time on the first bake of the evening.

The Koda 2 Pro lists 320F to 950F and the Volt 2 lists 70F to 850F. A wide range lets the oven roast and bake beyond pizza. If you only make pizza, the range matters less than recovery.  A wide range matters most if you roast or bake bread, and much less if pizza is the only job.  A good routine is to preheat, check the stone with a probe or gauge, and only then launch the first pie.

The Koda listings specify a 28 mBar regulator and hose. Check that it matches your tank connection before you order. A mismatch delays your first bake. Never improvise with unrated parts.  Keep the original box or a note of the regulator specification, because replacement parts are easiest to buy when you know the exact rating.  Keep any receipts and the serial number, since a warranty claim goes much faster with a clear record.

The Karu 12 asks for fire tending, while the Koda ovens light with a knob. The Volt 2 needs only a plug. If your evenings are short, gas or electric is the realistic choice.  Be honest about your routine, since an unused oven is the most expensive kind, whatever the fuel.  Write down your regular menu for a month before choosing, and match the oven to the dishes you actually make.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel and setting
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared propane, multi-fuel and electric designs by where each can run. The Volt 2 scored for indoor use, and the Koda ovens for convenience. We read this from the listings.  We also considered how clearly each listing states its fuel, regulator and setting limits.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stone and heat
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at stone claims and temperature ranges, from 850F on the Volt 2 to 950F on the Koda ovens. These are claims, not measurements. A thicker stone earned credit for recovery.  Where a listing gave a range instead of a single peak, we treated the range as the claim.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared chambers from 12 inches on the Karu to 18 inches on the Pro. Capacity affected the family-size score.  The warranty note on the Koda listing counted as a mild confidence signal.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls and monitoring
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the Connect hub on the Pro and the adaptive system on the Volt 2. More monitoring helps a beginner.  Monitoring tools such as the hub were weighed for how much they reduce guesswork.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed tier against capability. The Koda 2 sits in the middle, the Pro and Volt 2 higher, and the Karu 12 lower.  Value also reflected whether the oven works for more than pizza.

rows: Wood oven at a lower tier

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The Koda 2 and Koda 2 Pro light with a knob and recover quickly. You trade flame flavor for convenience. Choose gas for weeknights.

cards.label: Wood
cards.text: The Karu 12 burns wood or charcoal and offers smoke and a live fire. It needs tending and ash cleanup. Choose wood for weekends.

howToChoose.note: Busy households should pick gas. Hobbyists should pick wood.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An oven rated for indoor use, a manageable footprint and a good outlet. Never bring gas or wood ovens inside.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Ooni Volt 2 is the only model made for indoor use. The three outdoor ovens need open air.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You host often and want the Koda 2 Pro for large pies or the Volt 2 for indoor use.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You like fire and bake casually. The Karu 12 is a lower tier entry.

maintenance.why: Burnt flour smokes on the next cook. Dry brushing avoids cracks.  A soft brush is gentler than a metal scraper on the stone.  A thin coat of oil on bare steel parts helps in humid climates.
Cracks leak. Test connections with soapy water.  Replace any hose that looks stiff or shows surface cracks.  Soapy water and a small brush make leaks visible.
Ash blocks airflow and holds moisture. Remove it when cold.  Wear gloves and keep a metal bucket with a lid.  Dispose of ash in a metal container only.
Grease burns on at high heat. A damp cloth removes it.  Unplug the oven before wiping, and let it cool first.  Check the cord and plug for any wear.
Rain and sun age shells. A cover extends life.  Dry the shell fully so water does not pool in seams.  Store the cover dry to avoid mildew.

faq.q: Which Ooni is best for beginners?
faq.a: The Koda 2 is the easiest because it lights with a knob and holds steady heat. The Karu 12 takes fire skills. The Volt 2 is simplest if you cook indoors.  The Volt 2 is also the lowest-effort route if you worry about wind blowing out a gas flame.  Keep a simple checklist taped near the oven so every session starts safely.

faq.q: Can I use an Ooni indoors?
faq.a: Only the Volt 2 is designed for indoor use. The Koda and Karu ovens burn fuel and need open air. Never run them in a garage.  Always follow each manual's clearance and ventilation rules before the first fire.  Never leave a lit oven alone, and keep children and pets back.

Prices vary by tier, from the Karu 12 to the Koda 2 Pro. Spend more for size or indoor use. Check current listings because prices move.  Resale is strong for well-kept ovens, so a careful owner recovers part of the cost.  A cover also protects the stone from rain, which is a common cause of cracks.

Yes. A thicker stone stores more heat and recovers faster between pies. The Koda 2 lists a stone 50 percent thicker than before.  Dough hydration and flour type change the best heat, so use a recipe and keep notes.  Watch the stone color and flame as well as the number on the gauge.

The Koda listings include a 28 mBar regulator and hose. Confirm the connection matches your propane tank. Use only rated parts.  A wrong fitting is the common reason a first bake is delayed, so verify before you order.  A short note in your phone with the regulator rating saves a lot of searching later.

faq.q: How long does an Ooni last?
faq.a: Shells outlast hoses, motors and gaskets. A cover, dry storage and regular cleaning help. The maker lists a five year voluntary warranty on some models.  Replacement stones and covers are available separately, so a small yearly allowance covers upkeep.  A yearly inspection takes ten minutes and prevents most failures.
